title: Rav Huna
author: Aharon Hyman
attribution: English translation and editorial notes prepared for Joshua Waxman.

paragraphs: We know nothing about the parentage of this great man, who merited to occupy Rav’s seat at Sura. Rav Sherira Gaon, however, states in his Epistle, part III, at the end of chapter 2, that he belonged to the household of the nasi—that is, to the family of the exilarch. It is very plausible that he was a grandson of Rav Huna the exilarch, who died during Rabbi’s lifetime, as stated in Jerusalem Talmud, Kilayim 9:3.

Rav Sherira Gaon’s statement there that Rav Huna died in the year 608 of the era of contracts would enable us to calculate his year of birth: Mo’ed Katan 28a explicitly says that Rav Huna reached the age of eighty, which would put his birth in 528. More probably, however, “reached eighty” means that he lived considerably beyond eighty. The Gemara says only that, from eighty onward, a sudden death is a death by a divine kiss. He cannot have lived only eighty years: that would make him two when Rav came to Babylonia in 530, thirty at Rav’s death in 558, and only thirty-seven at Shmuel’s death in 565. Several of Rav’s students were then older than he, including Rav Yehuda, who was born when Rabbi died. Rav Chisda, too, who was a colleague-disciple of Rav Huna, was almost his age: he lived ninety-two years, as in Mo’ed Katan 28a, and died in 620, placing his birth in “קתכח.” Rather, Rav Huna certainly lived considerably beyond eighty and was approximately forty when Rav died. We find that he had already married off his son Rabba during Rav’s lifetime, and that he also had grown daughters, as in Megillah 27a. There he is described as a short man, extremely poor: once he had no wine for kiddush, so he pawned his belt, tied a rope around himself instead, and appeared before Rav. Rav asked what this meant; when he heard the story, he blessed him: “May it be God’s will that you be covered in silk.” So it happened. Apparently he worked the land and raised livestock. Megillah 28a describes Rav Huna carrying a hoe on his shoulder. When Rav Chana bar Chanilai wanted to take it from him and carry it, he replied: “If you are accustomed to carrying one in your own town, carry it; otherwise, I do not wish to gain honor through your humiliation.” In the Jerusalem Talmud, Sanhedrin 1:1, Rav Huna is tending animals when a man for whom he knows testimony asks him to come and testify. He answers that he will go if the man pays for his lost working time. On another occasion, someone comes to him for judgment while Rav Huna is picking fruit from a palm. He replies that he will hear the case if the man takes his place up the palm. Ketubot 105a likewise relates that he would tell litigants: “Give me a man to draw water in my place, and I will judge your case.” We thus see that he personally worked his land, watered his fields, gathered his fruit, and tended his animals.[^1]

None of this interfered with his study. He remained devoted to his beloved teacher and was a leading disciple of Rav. Shabbat 66b and 128a, Beitzah 40a, and Bava Kamma 115a explicitly say: “Was not Rav Huna Rav’s disciple?” He called Rav “Abba,” as in Pesachim 107a and Yoma 87a—an expression of esteem and authority.

He received most of his Torah from Rav. We find “Rav Huna said in Rav’s name” in Berakhot 49b; Shabbat 142b; Eruvin 7a, 30a, 85a, 87a; Pesachim 3b, 73a, 106b; Sukkah 2b; Beitzah 6b, 16b; Yoma 87a; Megillah 31a; Yevamot 17b, 59b, 60a, 88b, 93a; Ketubot 21b, 22a, 50b; Nazir 26b; Gittin 13a, 29a, 64b, 75b; Sotah 22a; Kiddushin 8a; Bava Kamma 21a, 30b, 106a; Bava Metzia 63a; Bava Batra 54a, 55a, 115b, 170b; Sanhedrin 28b; Chullin 19a, 57a, 133a; and Temurah 22b.
In the Jerusalem Talmud we find “Rabbi Chuna,” or “Rav Huna,” in Rav’s name: Shabbat 1:1; Eruvin 4:5; Megillah 1:1 and 2:2; and numerous other places.

In Chullin 95b he asks Rav a question, and Rav answers him playfully: “Do not be foolish in stringing things together.” Rav held him in such esteem that he authorized him to judge, as his son Rabba testifies in Sanhedrin 5a.

He also received teachings from Rav Asi, Rav Kahana’s colleague: “Rav Huna said in Rav Asi’s name,” in Bava Batra 126a and Chullin 19a. In Ketubot 48b, Rav Huna raises an objection to Rav Asi, and Rav says: “Did I not tell you not to follow a reversed teaching?” Tosafot, Berakhot 34a, s.v. *emtza’iyot*, likewise write that Rav Huna stood before Rav Asi as a disciple.

He also received teachings from Shmuel: “Rav Huna said in Shmuel’s name,” in Rosh Hashanah 32a, Sukkah 32b, and Kiddushin 6a. In Arakhin 16b, Rav Huna and Chiyya bar Rav sit before Shmuel. Where Gittin 5a and Zevachim 46b say that Shmuel asked Rav Huna a question, he may have been testing him; alternatively, that Rav Huna may be the exilarch who died during Rabbi’s lifetime. For “Rav Huna said that Rabbi Ze’ira said” in Berakhot 37a, Hyman specifies the reading אמר זעירא (“Ze’ira said”). We also find Rav Huna in Rabbi Chanina’s name in Shabbat 122a and Niddah 60b.
“Rav Huna said in Rabbi’s name” appears in Ketubot 68b. Where this wording occurs in Gittin 74a and Kiddushin 60b, it should read “in Rav’s name.”

“Rav Huna said in Rabbi Yannai’s name” appears in Chullin 122b. He also reports Rabbi Chiyya Rabba’s teaching in Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah 1:1 (2b), and at the end of 2:3. Since Rav Huna is known not to have been in the Land of Israel, we must say that he received these teachings from his teachers or from colleagues who came from the Land of Israel to Babylonia.

But the Rav Huna who sits before Rabbi Yirmeya in Shabbat 63b and Gittin 11b, and who asks Rabbi Ami a question in Bava Batra 11a, is a different Rav Huna, as we shall explain in the respective entries. Likewise, the Rav Huna who asks Rav Ashi questions in Shabbat 60b and Avodah Zarah 60b is the later Rav Huna.

When his holy teacher Rav died, all Rav’s leading students went to Shmuel at Neharde’a. Rav’s academy at Sura nevertheless continued; only the position of head of the academy was left unfilled, out of respect for Shmuel. A group of sages remained in Sura, with Rav Hamnuna supervising them, as explained in his entry, while Rav Huna was the greatest among them. Thus Sanhedrin 17b says that the expression “they say in Rav’s academy” means Rav Huna. It objects that Rav Huna himself says “they say in Rav’s academy,” and answers that the expression means Rav Hamnuna. Both statements are true. Yevamot 83b says: “Who is meant by ‘they say in Rav’s academy’? Rav Huna.” Rashi explains that although the answer there identifies Rav Hamnuna, that applies when Rav Huna himself says “they say in Rav’s academy”; when the expression occurs without qualification, it certainly means Rav Huna. Their intention is as we have explained: Rav Hamnuna was actually the supervisor of the study house at Sura, but Rav Huna was its greatest scholar. Everyone saw in him the future occupant of his teacher’s seat. As long as Rav Asi and Shmuel were alive, however, they all remained subordinate to them. Rav Asi did not live long after Rav, as in Niddah 36a. They sent all their questions to Shmuel, as in the recurring formula: “They sent from Rav’s academy to Shmuel: Let our master teach us.”

After Shmuel died, in 564 or 565, they began deliberating whom to appoint head of the academy, and where it should be—at Neharde’a, Shmuel’s home, or at Sura, Rav’s. Besides Rav Huna, there were leading disciples of Rav who were all worthy of the office: Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, who was virtually Rav’s colleague-disciple; Rav Yehuda, apparently older than Rav Huna, having been born on the day Rabbi died; and Rabba bar Avuha, Rav Nachman’s teacher. Three years passed before they agreed. Apparently they did not wish to establish the academy at Neharde’a because it stood on the frontier; perhaps they foresaw its destruction. It was indeed destroyed afterward, in 570, by Pappa bar Netzer, as recorded in Rav Sherira Gaon’s Epistle, III:2. Rav Yirmeya bar Abba apparently became head in Shum-Tamya, near Sura, as in Bava Batra 153a. Rav Yehuda founded a great academy at Pumbedita. But the principal academy, from which decisions and instruction went out to all Israel, was established at Sura, and the choice fell upon Rav Huna. All the virtues and good qualities were united in him. Besides his great wisdom—Rava later boasted that Rav Huna’s wisdom had been granted to him, in Mo’ed Katan 28a—he was immensely wealthy. As mentioned above, he had been very poor, but Rav blessed him and he became rich. Megillah 27b relates that Rav lived to see his blessing fulfilled: at the wedding of Rav Huna’s son Rabba, Rav Huna’s daughters and daughters-in-law came in. Rav Huna, who was short, was lying on his bed; they did not see him and covered him with silk. When Rav heard, he took exception and said: “Why, when I blessed him, did he not say, ‘And likewise to the master’?” Fortune smiled on Rav Huna, and he prospered in all his undertakings. Berakhot 5b relates that four hundred barrels of his wine once turned sour. Rav Yehuda, the brother of Rav Salla the Pious, and other rabbis—or, according to another account, Rav Adda bar Ahava and other rabbis—visited him and told him to examine his conduct. He asked anyone who had heard an accusation against him to state it. They answered that they had heard he was not giving his tenant the vine shoots due to him. He undertook to give them. Some say the vinegar became wine again—perhaps this is why Berakhot 57a says that one who sees Huna in a dream will experience a miracle—and others say the price of vinegar rose until it sold for the price of wine.

He also had an advantage over all his colleagues in belonging to the exilarch’s family. Rav Sherira Gaon teaches us this in his Epistle, III:2, where he says that Rav Huna belonged to the household of the nasi.

He was appointed head of the academy, to occupy Rav’s seat, [in 568]. Rav’s academy, however, had been in Sura itself, whereas Rav Sherira Gaon says that Rav Huna’s study house was near Mata Mechasya. As is known, several towns lay close together. A plausible conjecture is that his study house was in Derokart, which was near Mata Mechasya and Sura. We find Rav Nachman bar Rav Chisda there in Ta’anit 21b. This also explains the report there that a fire broke out in Derokart but not in Rav Huna’s neighborhood: people supposed that this was because Rav Huna’s merit was so great, but were told that this was a small matter for Rav Huna. All these towns were nevertheless reckoned under Sura’s name. Thus Sanhedrin 17b calls Rav Huna and Rav Chisda “the elders of Sura.” Rashi’s statement in Eruvin 62b that Rav Huna lived in Pumbedita is an evident scribal error.

Their hopes were not disappointed: they found the man they sought. He increased his academy sevenfold. Ketubot 106a relates that Rav Huna lectured through thirteen interpreters. When the rabbis rose from his academy and shook out their cloaks, the dust rose and obscured the sun, and people in the West would say: “They have risen from the academy of Rav Huna the Babylonian.” This is certainly figurative, but it shows how great his academy was: even in the Land of Israel his name was honored. The same passage says that the rabbis who remained there throughout the year numbered eight hundred. It is known that scholars assembled at the academy for examination only during the two months of the kallah. During the rest of the year they returned to their towns to work and studied at their own local academies; only the wealthy and the outstanding students remained continually with their master. He also had ten reciters of traditions in his academy, as implied by Horayot 3b.

Besides his many students, all Rav’s disciples sat before him and accepted his authority. Even his great colleagues—Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, Rav Yehuda, Rav Nachman, and their fellows—came to his academy to hear his decisions. Thus in Bava Batra 65b, where Rav Huna and Rav Yirmeya bar Abba disagree, Rav Yirmeya asks: “Many times I said before Rav that the law follows Rabbi Akiva, and he said nothing to me.” Rav Huna asks how he taught the dispute. He answers that he taught it with the positions reversed, and Rav Huna replies: “That is why he said nothing to you.” Likewise, in Bava Batra 170b, Rav Yirmeya bar Abba says that had Rav heard this baraita he would have retracted; Rav Huna answers that Rav had heard it and did not retract. We see clearly that Rav Yirmeya bar Abba, too, sought Rav Huna’s decision in interpreting the traditions received from their teachers. In Niddah 24b, Rav Yirmeya bar Abba proposes to act in accordance with Shmuel. Rav Huna asks whether he means to be stringent, and tells him that this is a stringency leading to leniency: he should at least follow Rav. They also disagree in Megillah 23a. This clearly shows that Rav Huna was not Rav Yirmeya bar Abba’s son, as one scholar wished to maintain.

We likewise find Rav Yehuda disagreeing with him in Bava Metzia 115a and Bava Batra 106a, with Rav Huna’s statement placed first. In Chullin 111b, Rav Kahana sits behind Rav Yehuda, while Rav Yehuda sits before Rav Huna. In Bekhorot 44a, Rav Huna gestures, “one of ours and one of theirs,” and Rav Yehuda takes offense; Rashi explains that Rav Yehuda was sitting opposite him. Yet Rav Huna esteemed him highly. In Chullin 19a, Rav Huna and Rav Yehuda disagree about Rav’s teaching. Rav Yehuda objects: “What I declare a terefa he permits, and what I permit he declares a terefa!” Rav Huna says that his anger is justified: first, Rav Yehuda heard the teaching directly from Rav, whereas he himself had not. In Kiddushin 70a, when Rav Nachman summons Rav Yehuda to appear before him in judgment, Rav Yehuda consults Rav Huna about whether to go. Rav Huna says: “You are not obliged to go, for you are a great man.” Thus Rav Sherira Gaon says in his Epistle, III:2: “Rav Yehuda headed the academy at Pumbedita, with his students before him, and would come to see Rav Huna from time to time.”

Although Rav Nachman calls him “our colleague Huna” in Kiddushin 47a and 78b, Bava Kamma 96b, Bava Batra 138b, Gittin 52b, and Chullin 56a, he was considerably younger than Rav Huna. He would continually come to Sura to resolve his doubts. He himself says in Niddah 28a: “It was explained to me by Rav Huna.” Likewise, Bava Batra 133a has Rav Nachman say, “And you told us concerning it”; he raises objections before Rav Huna in Zevachim 116b and Menachot 17a. We also find that Rav Nachman came to Sura in Sukkah 14b; Ketubot 94a and 99b; Bava Batra 132b; Shevuot 48b; and Chullin 19b. See his entry for a fuller account.
Rabba bar Avuha: when he became ill, Rav Huna and Rav Nachman visited him, as in Gittin 72a.

Rav Adda bar Ahava: Ta’anit 20b relates that Rav Huna had wine in a dilapidated building and wished to remove it, but feared that the building would fall. He brought Rav Adda bar Ahava inside and drew him into a discussion of a teaching until the wine had been removed. Once Rav Adda left, the building collapsed. When Rav Adda realized what had happened, he was angry. Nazir 57b relates that he asked Rav Huna: “Who shaves yours?” In Bava Kamma 80a he asks: “What about yours?”—meaning, who tends his small livestock. Rav Huna answers, “My wife Chova.” Rav Adda replies: “May Chova bury her children.” This was like an inadvertent error proceeding from a ruler, and throughout Rav Adda bar Ahava’s lifetime Rav Huna’s children by Chova did not survive.
They disagree in Nedarim 81a. In Jerusalem Talmud, Eruvin 4:3, Rav Huna reports in his name.

Rabbi Elazar, who was the leading authority in the Land of Israel, also deferred to him. In Bava Batra 125b he says: “This matter began with the great”—Rav Huna—“and ended with the small,” referring to himself.

Chiyya bar Rav: the two sat before Shmuel, as in Arakhin 16b, and Rav Huna questioned him in Ketubot 21b. Nevertheless, he called Rav Huna “my master,” in Bekhorot 22a. Their disagreements appear in Shabbat 69b and 135b; Bava Batra 4b; Avodah Zarah 49b; and Jerusalem Talmud, Eruvin 4:1.
Among his other colleagues was Rabbi Avin Naggara. Shabbat 23b says that Rav Huna regularly passed and repassed the entrance of Rabbi Avin Naggara’s house.
Rav Avya Sava: in Beitzah 21a, Rav Huna praises him as a great man.
Giddel bar Minyomi lived in his time. Bava Batra 31b relates that he found Rav Huna, Chiyya bar Rav, and Rav Chilkiya bar Tovi together, and lodged a protest before them.
Rav Giddel, Rav’s disciple, became infertile as a consequence of Rav Huna’s lectures, as in Yevamot 64b.[^2]
Geniva: in Gittin 31b, Rav Huna and Rav Chisda are sitting together when Geniva passes them.
Rav Chiyya bar Ashi: in Chullin 111b, they call one another “orphan.”
Rav Chilkiya bar Tovya: they sit together in Bava Batra 39a.
Rav Chanan bar Rava tells Rav Huna in Eruvin 6a: “Do not disagree with me.” Rav Chananel: in Bekhorot 24b, when Rav Huna is asked a question, he tells them to go and ask Rav Chananel.
Rabbi Yitzchak: their disagreement appears in Eruvin 17a.

Rav Chisda was Rav Huna’s colleague-disciple. We find that he issued rulings during Rav Huna’s lifetime at Kafri, as in Eruvin 62b. Rav Huna told him: “Your name is Chisda, and your words are gracious,” in Gittin 7a. In Bava Metzia 33a, Rav Chisda asks Rav Huna about a disciple whose teacher needs him. Rav Huna suspects that Rav Chisda means himself, and replies: “Chisda, Chisda, I do not need you until forty years have passed,” and so forth.

In fact, Rav Chisda was almost as old as Rav Huna. Rav Sherira Gaon’s Epistle, III:2, states that Rav Chisda died in 620, ten years after Rav Huna. Rav Chisda is known to have lived ninety-two years, as stated in Mo’ed Katan 28a. He constantly sat before Rav Huna, whom he calls “the master” in Sukkah 14b and Chullin 19a, and “my pure master” in Chullin 90b. He raises objections before Rav Huna in Berakhot 22a and Pesachim 73a. Rav Huna esteemed him so much that he instructed his son Rabba: “Why are you not regularly with Rav Chisda? His teachings are incisive,” in Shabbat 82a.[^1]

Their disagreements appear in Berakhot 25a; Shabbat 146a; Sukkah 50b; Beitzah 14a; Ketubot 24b and 50a; Sotah 5a; Gittin 64a; Bava Batra 31b; and Chullin 10a. In Berakhot 24b, Rav Huna reports a teaching in Rabbi Yochanan’s name, and Rav Chisda says: “By God, even if Rabbi Yochanan told it to me with his own mouth, I would not listen to him.” The wording in Pesachim 107a, “Rav Huna asked Rav Chisda,” is a scribal error and should be reversed, as in the readings of Bach and Dikdukei Soferim.
Ratsi bar Yechezkel sends Rav Huna a message in Shabbat 138a: “Tell us, master, those excellent things you told us in Rav’s name.”[^3]
Mar Ukva lived in his time. In Mo’ed Katan 20b Rav Huna asks him: “Do you wish to eat tzudnayata (צודנייתא)?”[^7]
**His students and those who reported in his name**

Rabbi Abba asks Rav Huna questions in Nazir 13a; Sotah 8b; Chullin 40a; and Niddah 12a. He sits before him in Bava Kamma 120a. Rabbi Abba reports Rav Huna’s teachings in Shabbat 5a, 41a, 113b; Sukkah 13b; Yevamot 98a; Ketubot 21b, 104b; Nedarim 77a; Gittin 6a, 63b, 80b, 89a; Kiddushin 70b; Bava Metzia 47a, 107b; Sanhedrin 30b; and Chullin 133a. On coming to the Land of Israel, Rabbi Abba boasted to Rabbi Ze’ira: “By the master’s life, from the day the master came up here, we had an opportunity to speak before Rav Huna, and we questioned him,” as in Chullin 57b.

Rabbi Abba bar Zavda became infertile as a consequence of Rav Huna’s lectures, as in Yevamot 64b. Where Ketubot 7a reads “Rabbi Chelbo said that Rav Huna said that Rabbi Abba bar Zavda said,” the order should be reversed: “Rabbi Abba bar Zavda said that Rav Huna said.”
Shmuel’s father: in Me’ilah 9a he raises an objection to Rav Huna. But that is the earlier Rav Huna, the exilarch who died in Rabbi’s lifetime.
Avimi of Hagrunya reports in his name in Yevamot 64b.
Rabbi Avina was his student, as in Gittin 66a.
Rav Acha Arikha reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Menachot 35b.
Rav Acha bar Akha sits before Rav Huna in Chullin 49a.
Rav Acha bar Yosef questions Rav Huna in Shabbat 140a.

Rav Acha bar Yaakov says in Yevamot 64b: “We were sixty elders, and all became infertile as a consequence of Rav Huna’s lectures, except for me, for I fulfilled in myself, ‘Wisdom preserves its possessor’s life,’” and so forth.
Achi the irrigator says: “I carried Rav Huna”—in a litter on a festival—“from Hini to Shili,” in Beitzah 25b.
Rabbi Aivu bar Naggara reports in his name in Jerusalem Talmud, Sukkah 4:3.

Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi, the distinguished priests of the Land of Israel, were subordinate to Rav Huna, as in Megillah 22a and Gittin 59b. In Mo’ed Katan 25a they say: “When we were there, we did not dare raise our heads before him.” Their disagreement appears in Pesachim 55b.
Rav Daniel bar Rav Ketina reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Ketubot 97a and Jerusalem Talmud, Eruvin 1:10.
Rav Huna bar Chiyya received teachings from him, as in Bava Batra 111a.
Rav Hoshaya questions the elder Rav Huna in Bekhorot 37b. In the same tractate, 17a, he tells Rabba: “When you go in before Rav Huna, ask him.”

Rav Hamnuna II was his student, as in Eruvin 63a. Kiddushin 29b relates that Rav Chisda praised Rav Hamnuna to Rav Huna as a great man, and Rav Huna asked that he be brought to him. When he came, Rav Huna saw that he was not wearing a head-covering cloth and asked why. Rav Hamnuna said that he was unmarried. Rav Huna turned his face away and told him: “See that you do not appear before me until you marry.”
Rav Zavdi reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Arakhin 13b.

Rabbi Ze’ira was his student. In Menachot 29a he says: “It was explained to me by Rav Huna.” In Berakhot 39a he says: “When we were at Rav Huna’s academy,” and so forth. Rabbi Ze’ira reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Bava Kamma 9a and Chullin 57b. Jerusalem Talmud, Berakhot 4:2, has “Rabbi Ze’ira in Rav Huna’s name.” The same wording survives in Ta’anit 11b: “Rabbi Ze’ira said that Rav Huna said.” In Jerusalem Talmud, Shabbat 7:2—28, he reports several teachings in his name.
Rabbi Zerika reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Sotah 21b.
Rav Chana attended him, as in Mo’ed Katan 25a.
Rav Chiyya Arikha recites a teaching before him in Berakhot 33a, according to the reading in Dikdukei Soferim.
Rabbi Chiyya bar Avin reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Ta’anit 8a, Ketubot 48a, and Kiddushin 27a. He asks Rav Huna questions in Shabbat 140a and Kiddushin 58a.

Rabbi Chelbo reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Berakhot 6b and 62b, Megillah 4b and 29b, and Mo’ed Katan 26a. He became infertile as a consequence of Rav Huna’s lectures, as in Yevamot 64b. He says, “I saw Rav Huna,” and so forth, in Menachot 32b. Jerusalem Talmud, Megillah 1:1, has “Rabbi Chelbo, Rabbi Chuna in Rav’s name.”
Rav Chana bar Chinena asks Rav Huna a question in Pesachim 106b.

Rav Chana bar Chanilai calls Rav Huna “the master” in Megillah 27a and comes before him in Beitzah 40a. Megillah 28a relates that Rav Huna once carried a hoe on his shoulder. Rav Chana bar Chanilai saw him and wanted to carry it for him, but Rav Huna would not allow it, refusing to gain honor through his humiliation.
Rav Chanan bar Molada reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Sanhedrin 70a.
Chanan Bisha lived in his time, as in Bava Kamma 115a.
Rav Yehuda, the brother of Rav Salla the Pious, calls Rav Huna “the master” in Berakhot 5b.
Rav Huna issued a ruling to the brother of Rav Yehuda bar Zavdi, in Jerusalem Talmud, Mo’ed Katan 3:4.
Rabbi Yosei bar Chanina reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Berakhot 52b. Their disagreement appears in Ketubot 63a.

Rav Yosef was his leading disciple. He says, “When I was at Rav Huna’s academy,” in Shabbat 129b. Rav Yosef sits before Rav Huna in Eruvin 7a, Sukkah 11a, Bava Kamma 102a, Avodah Zarah 7a, and Chullin 74a. He questions Rav Huna in Berakhot 25b.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Ashyan reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Sukkah 42a and Gittin 39a.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Chanina reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Ketubot 4b. In the same tractate, 61a, and in Nedarim 38b, the patronymic is “bar Chananya.”
Rabbi Yitzchak, the son of Rav Yehuda, studied the tractate Niddah at Rav Huna’s academy, as in Niddah 17b.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Marta reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Pesachim 33b.
Rabbi Yitzchak bar Redifa reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Shabbat 23b.
Rav Yitzchak bar Shmuel bar Marta reports Rav Huna’s teaching and questions him in Ketubot 21b.
Rav Kahana raises an objection before Rav Huna in Mo’ed Katan 13b. In Chullin 111b, Rav Kahana sits behind Rav Yehuda, before Rav Huna. In Eruvin 105a Rav Huna says: “Kahana assists the priests.”

Levi bar Buti was reading the curses before Rav Huna and hesitated. Rav Huna told him: “Take them upon yourself,” and so forth, in Megillah 31b. In the Jerusalem Talmud there, 3:8, the name is Levi bar Panti.
Rav Menashe bar Zevid appears before Rav Huna in Yevamot 19b.
Rav Menashya bar Gadda reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Sukkah 13b.
Mar Zutra expounds in Rav Huna’s name in Eruvin 41b.
Mari bar Mar: in Gittin 86b, Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sends Mari bar Mar to ask Rav Huna a question, but Rav Huna dies in the meantime.
Na’ali reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Chullin 45b.

Rav Sechora reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Berakhot 5a and 26a; Shabbat 24a; Yevamot 106a; Bava Kamma 21a; Sanhedrin 49b; and Menachot 40b. Rava: we find “Rava said to Rav Huna” in Shabbat 54a. Although Tosafot, Bekhorot 14a, write that Rava did not see Rav Huna, this follows the reading that Rava was born when Rav Yehuda died. On that reading, Rava was born two years after Rav Huna’s death. But we have already explained Rambam’s reading: “Before Rav Yehuda died, Rava was born.” Rava actually lived approximately seventy-four years and died in 663, as explained in Rav Sherira Gaon’s Epistle, part “ח״נ,” chapter 2. Thus, when Rav Huna died in 608, Rava was more than twenty years old, and it is very plausible that he had the opportunity to speak with him. Rava was, however, Rav Nachman’s leading disciple at Neharde’a and did not come to Sura. We therefore find him speaking with Rav Huna only incidentally. This is why Rava asks Rafram bar Pappa, in Ta’anit 20b, to relate the fine deeds Rav Huna performed. Rafram tells him what Rav Huna did in his old age. We likewise find in Pesachim 114b that Rava sought beet greens and rice because these had been mentioned by Rav Huna. But in Jerusalem Talmud, Kilayim 1:9, “Rava in Rav Huna’s name” should certainly read “Rabbi Ba in Rav Huna’s name.”[^4]
Rava bar Chilkai—“Chakuka” in Dikdukei Soferim—asks Rav Huna a question in Eruvin 67b.

Rabba was his leading disciple. In Eruvin 17a he says: “I asked Rav Huna”; in Menachot 36a: “Rav Huna explained it to me”; and in Eruvin 40a and 40b: “When we were at Rav Huna’s academy.” In Yevamot 61b, Gittin 27a, and Bava Batra 172b, Rav Chisda tells Rabba: “Go and examine it, for this evening Rav Huna will ask you about it.” In Bekhorot 17a Rav Hoshaya tells him: “When you go in before Rav Huna, ask him.” In Nazir 42b Rabba reports Rav Huna’s teaching.
Rabba bar Natan asks Rav Huna a question in Bava Kamma 32a.
Rami bar Abba reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Eruvin 10a and 61a.

Rami bar Chama reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Eruvin 5; Rosh’s reading is Rami bar Abba. In Zevachim 18b, Rav Huna comes to Argiza, and his host’s son poses a difficulty to him. He replies: “Leave that aside; Rami bar Chama treated that case differently.” This cannot be correct. The reading of Tzon Kodashim, “Rabba bar Rav Huna,” is preferable; alternatively, this may be the third Rav Huna, as explained below.
Rami bar Shmuel studied Niddah at Rav Huna’s academy, as in Niddah 17b.
Rav Sheizvi reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Bekhorot 11a.
Rav Shmuel bar Sheva reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Shevuot 17b.
Rav Shmuel bar Yitzchak recites teachings before Rav Huna in Megillah 8b and Bava Batra 113b, and questions him in Eruvin 36a.

Rav Sheshet was his leading disciple. He himself tells Rav Anan in Ketubot 69b that Rav Huna is his teacher. He became infertile as a consequence of Rav Huna’s lectures, in the same tractate, 64b. Bava Metzia 72b has Rav Sheshet reporting Rav Huna’s teaching. Where Pesachim 102b reads “Rav Huna said in Rav Sheshet’s name,” that is Rav Huna bar Yehuda, according to Rif’s reading.
Rav Tachlifa says: “I saw Rav Huna,” and so forth, in Mo’ed Katan 25a.
Rabbi Tanchum reports Rav Huna’s teaching in Mo’ed Katan 16b.
Rav Huna took pride neither in his wealth nor in his Torah and wisdom. His entire desire and purpose was to support the poor, as stated in Megillah 27a.

Not for nothing was he called “the pious man of Babylonia,” in Ta’anit 23b: he truly was exceptionally pious. Horayot 3b relates that when Rav Huna went out to court, he brought ten reciters from Rav’s academy before him, “so that only a splinter of the beam would reach us”—that is, to share responsibility for judgment. Thus he says in Berakhot 6a that the words of anyone who fears Heaven are heeded, and that one who knows his fellow is accustomed to greet him should greet him first. He personally lit the lamp in honor of Shabbat, as in Shabbat 119a; he learned this practice from Rabbi Avin Naggara, as in Shabbat 23b. He called his students “my masters,” in Berakhot 22a.

When he heard a pleasing teaching from Rav Chisda, he told him: “Your name is Chisda, and your words are gracious,” as in Gittin 7a. Once Rav Chisda objected to his statement, Rav Huna told him that Rav Adda bar Ahava supported his position, in Berakhot 22a. When Rav Nachman asked whether the law followed “our view or yours,” Rav Huna answered: “It follows yours, for you are close to the gate of the exilarch,” in Bava Batra 85a. When Rav Yehuda took offense, Rav Huna said his anger was justified: he had heard the teaching from Rav, whereas Rav Huna had not, in Chullin 19a. He told Shmuel: “Heaven forbid that Rav’s offspring should be put to shame through me,” in Arakhin 16b. Once he suspected Rav Chisda without cause and afterward fasted forty fasts for having done so, in Bava Metzia 33a. His student Rav Chaggi testified that once his tefillin strap turned over, and he fasted forty fasts for it, in Mo’ed Katan 25a. Once he answered Rav Avya Sava jokingly, “A raven flew!” His son Rabba asked: “Does not the master praise him as a great man?” Rav Huna acknowledged his son’s point and answered: “What can I do? Today I need to be sustained with cakes,” in Beitzah 21a. He instructed his son Rabba: “Why are you not regularly with Rav Chisda? His teachings are incisive,” in Shabbat 82a.

On one occasion, however, we find him insisting on the honor due to his Torah. Ketubot 69a relates that Rav Anan sent him this message: “Peace to our colleague Huna. When this woman comes before you, collect for her a tenth of the estate.” Rav Sheshet was sitting before him. Rav Huna took particular offense at being called “our colleague Huna”; perhaps he also knew of the incident in Ketubot 78b, where Rav Anan called Rav Nachman “Nachman the farmer.” He therefore sent his student Rav Sheshet, making him swear not to alter his words, with the message: “Anan, Anan! Is it collected from land or from movable property? And who sits first in a house of mourning?” When Rav Sheshet came before Rav Anan, he sought to appease him: “The master is great, and Rav Huna is the master of the master. But my teacher has placed me under a ban if I do not repeat his words, so I must tell you what he said.” Rav Anan was very angry and came to Mar Ukva to complain that Rav Huna had addressed him as “Anan, Anan,” and that he did not even understand the further question sent to him. Mar Ukva replied: “Would a man who does not know what a *marze’acha*, a house of mourning, is send to Rav Huna and call him ‘our colleague Huna’?”

As long as Rabbi Yochanan was alive in the Land of Israel, Rav Huna was the greatest authority of the generation only in Babylonia. But when Rabbi Yochanan died in 599, toward the end of Rav Huna’s life, all the sages of the Land of Israel also accepted Rav Huna as their head. As mentioned above, Rabbi Elazar deferred to him, and Rabbi Ami and R’ Ashi were subordinate to Rav Huna, as in Gittin 59b. Thus Jerusalem Talmud, Chagigah 1:8, calls Rav Huna “head of all the tribes.” He was called to the Torah in the place of a priest, although he was an Israelite, as in Gittin 59b. Despite all his many responsibilities, he found time to write seventy Torah scrolls—or, more correctly, seven, according to Dikdukei Soferim—as in Bava Batra 14a.[^5]

In Ta’anit 20b, Rava asks Rafram bar Pappa to tell him about Rav Huna’s great deeds. He answers: “I do not remember his youth; I remember his old age.” Every cloudy day, they would take Rav Huna out in a golden litter, and he would inspect the entire town. He would demolish every unstable wall, and if its owners could not afford to rebuild it, he rebuilt it at his own expense. Every Friday he sent agents to the market, bought all the vegetables the gardeners had left over, and threw them into the river. When he ate bread, he opened his door and announced: “Whoever is in need, let him come and eat.” Rava said that he could fulfill all these practices except this last one.
**His wife, sons, and daughters**

Nazir 57b and Bava Kamma 80a give his wife’s name as Chova. Rav Adda bar Ahava once asked Rav Huna, “Who shaves yours?” and, “What about yours?” He answered, “Chova.” Rav Adda said: “May Chova bury her children.” The sages say that throughout Rav Adda bar Ahava’s lifetime, Rav Huna’s children by her did not survive. It is very plausible that Chova was Rav Huna’s second wife. The children she bore did not survive, but his first wife bore him Rabba, as well as other sons and daughters, as in Megillah 27b. He had much satisfaction from them, particularly from his son Rabba, to whom he transmitted his Torah, as in Berakhot 53b, Mo’ed Katan 20a, Chullin 57a, and Me’ilah 15b according to the reading in Shittah Mekubbetzet. Rav Huna told him: “My son, you possess purity,” as in Sotah 49. Rabba repeatedly said, “Thus said my father and master,” in Gittin 29b and Bava Kamma 21a and 97a. His father authorized him to judge, as in Sanhedrin 5a.
**His death and resting place**

His death is mentioned in Gittin 86b: Rabbi Abba bar Zavda sent Mari bar Mar to ask Rav Huna, but Rav Huna died in the meantime. Mo’ed Katan 28a says that Rav Huna died suddenly. The rabbis were troubled, until Zuga of Hadayav taught them that this concern applied only to one who had not reached eighty; after eighty, it was a death by a divine kiss. As explained above, he lived considerably beyond eighty. Mo’ed Katan 25a relates that when Rav Huna died they considered placing a Torah scroll on his bier. Rav Chisda objected: “Shall we now do for him something he disapproved of in his lifetime?” Rav Tachlifa had said: “I saw Rav Huna about to sit on a bed on which a Torah scroll lay; he turned a jar over on the ground and placed the scroll on it.” The bier would not pass through the doorway. They considered lowering it through the roofs or transferring him to another bed, but Rav Chisda would not allow this. He said he had learned from Rav Huna that a sage’s honor requires going through the doorway and on the original bed. They broke open the doorway and took him out. His student Rabbi Abba eulogized him: “Our master was worthy that the Divine Presence should rest upon him, but Babylonia prevented it.”

His coffin was taken up to the Land of Israel. Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi went out to meet it, but Rabbi Ila and Rabbi Chanina did not, because they thought his body was no longer intact. Kohelet Rabbah 9:10 relates that Rav Huna directed that he be buried in the Land of Israel beside Rabbi Chiyya Rabba. There, however, he is called Rav Huna the exilarch, as he is also in Jerusalem Talmud, Kilayim 9:4. The meaning is that he belonged to the exilarch’s family, or that he was head of the entire exile. They discussed where to lay him: Rav Huna had disseminated Torah in Israel, and Rabbi Chiyya had disseminated Torah in Israel. They asked who would take him in. Rav Chagga said: “I will take him in, because I established my learning before him, recited it before him, and know his conduct. Once his tefillin strap turned over, and he fasted forty fasts for it.” Kilayim 9:4 says that Rav Chagga was then eighty years old. When he brought the coffin beside Rabbi Chiyya and his sons, a pillar of fire arose. Rav Chagga saw it and was frightened; he stood Rav Huna’s coffin upright and went out.[^6]
His great student Rav Chisda succeeded him, after Rav Yehuda’s death, which occurred two years after Rav Huna’s, as explicitly stated in Rav Sherira Gaon’s Epistle, III:2.

notes.text: The dates are given in the era of contracts, or Seleucid era. The text prints the unusual sequence קתכח in the birth calculation. It dates Rav Huna’s death to 608, but also says that Rav Chisda died in 620, ten years after him; these figures do not agree exactly.
The expression איעקר or איעקור is understood here as becoming infertile, rather than as leaving the lectures.
The Hebrew text spells this name רצי, transliterated here as Ratsi; the name is uncertain.
A death in 663 at approximately seventy-four would place Rava at about nineteen in 608, although the narrative says that he was more than twenty.
This paragraph reads “R’ Ashi.” Earlier, the same entry names Rabbi Ami and Rabbi Asi together. The two readings have been kept distinct.
The entry uses the forms Chaggi (חגי) and Chagga (חגא) in different passages.
The Aramaic food term צודנייתא (tzudnayata) is left without a more specific identification.
